p: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
